description: We’re a dedicated and hardworking team of first-year engineering students at Tecnológico de Monterrey Sonora Norte.
summary: When long missions take astronauts farther from Earth, crews need to notice health changes and act while support from the ground may be delayed. For the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge, we built NOMAD, a Windows workstation for astronauts and crew medical officers. It combines a guided daily check-in, six health indicators, symptom mapping, a journal and motor tests in a record organized by crew member and mission stage. Crews can review trends and prepare a handoff. Ham, the onboard assistant, runs Qwen locally through Ollama and retrieves relevant passages from an importable library of NASA research and mission references. Recognized urgent reports trigger a built-in alert before a model response. We built the prototype with C# WinForms, WebView2 and JavaScript. Two synthetic crew histories let judges try the workflow on a local PC.
details:
What NOMAD does

NOMAD gives astronauts a repeatable way to record changes in how they feel and work during long missions. The crew medical officer can review what changed, when it started, and which observations belong to that mission stage.

How the crew uses it

  1. Choose a crew profile and mission stage. Earth Orbit, Moon, Mars, Deep Space and Earth are available. The current stage is shared across the installation, and saved records retain their original stage.
  2. Complete a guided check-in. Enter heart rate (bpm), blood pressure (mmHg), temperature (°C), blood glucose (mg/dL), sleep (hours) and mood (1–10). Record symptoms and how they affect duties. The daily routine also offers an optional photo, a journal and motor exercises that record reaction and coordination measures. The demo labels its ARChER readings as simulated.
  3. Review changes and follow up. Health shows the latest indicators and interactive daily, 7-day and 30-day trends. Select a body region to record a symptom. Records brings together dated observations, check-ins and motor results for review or export.
  4. Consult the mission library. Import the research folder through Documents. When a crew member asks Ham a reference question, NOMAD ranks relevant Markdown passages, sends selected passages to Qwen and lets the crew open the evidence beside its answer.

A reproducible crew scenario

Open the Maya Chen demo in Earth Orbit and enter a simulated report of fatigue after a shift change. Review her sleep trend and the dated check-in together, then ask Ham how an irregular schedule can affect a shift. Inspect the linked reference passage. In a separate simulated drill, reporting an unresponsive crewmate triggers an immediate onboard alert and can surface a reported breathing observation for the crew medical officer.

Architecture and evaluation

C# WinForms hosts the JavaScript interface in Microsoft Edge WebView2. Profile and health records are stored on the workstation. IndexedDB holds daily photos and imported documents. Ollama serves Qwen over the local loopback interface, allowing the app and model to run locally after setup. The Windows build includes two synthetic astronaut profiles, each with 30 days of sample history. The full research collection contains 503 Markdown documents. Eleven automated scenario tests passed, covering emergency handling, demo readings and check-in behavior. These are software checks. Operational use requires clinical validation and mission approval.

Use of Language Model

Ham uses Qwen3 4B through Ollama for follow-up questions, summaries, source-backed explanations and extracting reported observations for emergency handoffs. Recognized urgent reports trigger an alert before model processing. The optional Qwen3-VL 4B workflow uses synthetic ultrasound images for training demonstrations. ChatGPT (Codex) assisted with source verification, submission writing and slide preparation.
